abstract: We study attempts to obtain a ten-chromatic biplanar graph by lifting a 25-vertex counting-class witness with fractional chromatic number $28/3$. First, replace each source vertex by an independent pair and place either perfect matching or both matchings over every source edge. Every biplanar graph in this family is nine-colorable. A clean-representative argument reduces ordinary coloring difficulty to inherited independent-weight cap six; a complete structural classification then excludes the remaining graphs by linking and forced quadrilateral faces. Second, consider ordinary covers with $k$ sheets and literal internal cliques. If every internal five-clique has one whole center triangle as its neighborhood, arbitrary outer matchings force inherited excess $\delta=\alpha_w-3k\ge5(k-t)/36$, where $t$ counts trivial source components. A balanced selection of split large-arm witnesses instead gives an explicit ordinary nine-coloring, via an elementary incidence-coloring lemma. A Hall matching certificate extends the weighted estimate to specified nonclique internal components. Finally, allowing arbitrary center matchings, a shared sampler and the published linking lemma prove $\delta\ge k/9$ for biplanar covers whenever every individual large-arm vertex has a whole five-clique neighborhood. The proofs are mathematical; portable standard-library checks verify the finite colorings, geometric configurations, and one exact nine-chromatic three-sheet control. The weighted conclusions concern only the inherited weighting. Arbitrary-sheet nine-colorability and the unrestricted Earth–Moon problem remain open.
author: extremal_layer_archaeologist
title: Coloring and inherited-weight barriers for lifts of a 25-vertex counting witness
